The caption is loose; the provenance claim repeats it as fact.
units.fix: ...a table of base percentages (a sample of Chargaff's 1952 data, with a later φX174 row added) covers maize, octopus, ... and E. coli, and φX174, whose unequal A and T mark single-stranded DNA

units.evidence: [W11.8] 'the four frequencies were not equal, with variations consistent between different studies'; [W11.10] [W11.11]; [W11.12] 'there was no reason why the sequence could not store information'
units.note: Two slips against the cited source: (1) 'varied between species' is not in the Tetranucleotide page ('consistent between different studies' is about reproducibility, not species); it is true and pinned elsewhere at [W5.55]. (2) 'its sequence could store information' upgrades the source's double negative ('no reason why ... could not') into a positive finding.
units.fix: Chargaff showed the four base frequencies were unequal, so DNA was not a systematic repeat and nothing stopped its sequence from storing information; G = C and A = T suggested the bases were paired (add cite Avery–MacLeod–McCarty [W5.55] for 'varied between species')
units.resolved: Now “nothing stopped its sequence from storing information”, without the species claim; a new provenance entry cites [W5.55] (Avery–MacLeod–McCarty) for variation by species.

units.resolved: Now ends “that is transcribed to produce RNA”.

units.evidence: [W1.19] 'Before typical cell division, these chromosomes are duplicated'; [W13.1]
units.note: 'before a cell divides, all of it is copied' drops the source's 'typical': the second meiotic division happens with no copying. Secondary (general knowledge): the Meselson–Stahl runs were done in 1957 and published in 1958; '1958' matches the source.
units.fix: Every gene you carry is a stretch of DNA, and before a cell divides in the usual way, all of it is copied.

units.evidence: [W1.8] base pairing rules (A with T and C with G)
units.note: 'always' ignores rare mismatches ([W2.51]); acceptable teaching simplification. 'In the same order' sidesteps antiparallel reading, and no option is the reverse complement, so it is unambiguous.
Complement of A T G C C A is T A C G G T: checked letter by letter.
Distractor is the original strand; feedback correct.
G C A T T G against A T G C C A pairs A–G and T–C (and G–A, C–T); feedback describes it correctly.
Key T A C G G T is the only correct position-by-position complement.
C G T A A C pairs A–C and T–G; feedback names A–C only, which is enough.
'sinks lower' is a fair simplification of banding at equal density in a CsCl gradient [W13.22]; source says 'several generations', 'many' is fine.

units.evidence: [W13.27] 'conservative replication would result in equal amounts of DNA of the higher and lower densities (but no DNA of an intermediate density)'
[W13.26] 'After one replication, the DNA was found to have intermediate density.'

units.note: The answer is rightly wrong, but the feedback's reason presupposes the conclusion: under the conservative model one of the two copies (the old molecule) contains no new material and is exactly as heavy as the original. A learner weighing conservative copying gets a circular rebuttal. The model-neutral reason is that half of all the DNA is now new and light.
units.fix: All at the heavy mark — feedback: Half of all the DNA after one round is newly built from light nitrogen, so it cannot all sit at the heavy mark.
units.resolved: Feedback now: after one round, half of all the DNA is newly built from light nitrogen, so it can’t all sit at the heavy mark.

units.evidence: [W13.28] 'this result was consistent with both semiconservative and dispersive replication'
units.note: Overclaims round one. The single middle band only rules out conservative copying; mixing old and new pieces along every strand (dispersive) gives the same band. Stating 'the two old strands came apart ... so every copy is a hybrid' as the explanation after round one teaches that round one proved semiconservative copying, which the source explicitly says it did not.
units.fix: ...Meselson and Stahl saw exactly this. Copying that mixed old and new pieces along every strand would also give one middle band; the next round tells the two apart.
units.resolved: Now says one middle band matches semiconservative copying but also dispersive copying, and the next round tells them apart.

units.evidence: [W13.32] dispersive would give 'a single density, lower than the intermediate density'; [W13.31]
units.note: Distractor and first sentence are right, but the rebuttal's causal link is a non sequitur: an old heavy strand that 'stays whole and gets a light partner' makes another hybrid, not a light molecule. The fully light band comes from the light strands made in round one getting light partners.
units.fix: ...Instead each strand stays whole and gets a new light partner, so the light strands made in round one give fully light copies: a second, light band appears.
units.resolved: Now: each strand stays whole and gets a new light partner, so the light strands made in the first round give fully light copies.

units.evidence: [W13.31] 'equal amounts of DNA with two different densities, one ... intermediate ... the other ... 14N'

units.note: Fine in context: after round one there is no heavy duplex left to persist, and every new strand is light.

units.evidence: [W4.39] polymerase adds nucleotides 'matched to the template strand, one at a time, via the creation of phosphodiester bonds'; [W4.10] replication forks; [W1.219]
units.note: The sequence 'strands come apart → loose letters line up along each old strand → the lined-up letters are linked' teaches a known misconception: that free nucleotides align along a whole template and are zipped together afterwards. In cells the strands open progressively at a fork and each nucleotide is linked by the polymerase as it pairs. The key order is still the only sensible one.
units.fix: Step 2: 'A new letter pairs with the next letter on each old strand, A facing T and C facing G'; Step 3: 'It is linked onto the end of the growing new strand'.
units.resolved: Steps 2–3 now: a new letter pairs with the next letter on each old strand; it is linked onto the end of the growing strand. Explanation matched.

units.evidence: [W5.25] 'an enzyme preparation of "deoxyribonucleodepolymerase" (a crude preparation ...) destroyed the extract's transforming power'; [W5.34] Mirsky's contamination challenge; [W5.60]
units.note: Key and claim ('pointed to DNA') are right. The explain overreaches: a crude enzyme preparation could carry other activities (exactly Mirsky's objection), so the result made DNA the likeliest carrier; it did not mean the carrier 'had to be' DNA. The explain names the enzyme crude and then draws a certain conclusion from it.
units.fix: ...Only a crude enzyme that breaks down DNA destroyed its power, which pointed to DNA as the carrier of the change.
units.resolved: Explanation now ends “which pointed to DNA as the carrier of the change”.

units.evidence: [W3.5] [W3.47]; [W1.54] 'Modified bases occur in DNA'; [W1.56] noncanonical bases in bacteriophages; [W1.63] 5-Hydroxymethyldeoxyuracil
units.note: Key is the best answer, but two distractors can be argued right, and the claim overgeneralizes. (1) 'It contains a fifth kind of letter': only A and T are given, so a T-substitute such as 5-hydroxymethyluracil (or uracil) pairing with A in a double strand would give exactly A > T; the pinned DNA source lists such bases in phage DNA. (2) 'Two strands of different lengths' is a partly single-stranded molecule, the same mechanism as the key. Claim 'Unequal shares of A and T mean the DNA has no partner strand' is stated as a certainty; 'suggest' (as the stem says) is right.
units.fix: Replace 'It contains a fifth kind of letter' with 'Its G and C must be unequal too' and 'It has two strands of different lengths' with 'Its strands pair A with A'; claim: 'In double-stranded DNA A equals T, so a big gap between them points to a single strand.'
units.resolved: Distractors replaced with “Its G and C must be unequal too” and “Its strands pair A with A”; claim and explanation now say a gap points to a single strand.

units.evidence: [W6.16] [W6.17] [W6.20] 'performed once for the sulfur-labeled phages and once for phosphorus-labeled phages'; [W6.41] [W6.42] [W6.25]; [W8.56] 'Not all genomes are DNA (e.g. RNA viruses)'
units.note: Key 'Mostly the phosphorus' and the current explain are right. The claim is wrong as written: (1) it inverts the inference ('Since genes are DNA, ... DNA enters') when the experiment is evidence FOR genes being DNA; (2) it generalizes to every virus and 'the cell it infects', which is false: RNA viruses carry no DNA, and many animal viruses enter cells whole, protein coat included. Secondary: the stem reads as one phage tagged both ways; Hershey and Chase labelled separate batches [W6.20].
units.fix: Claim: 'In Hershey and Chase's experiment the phage's DNA, not its protein coat, entered the bacteria: evidence that its genes were DNA.' Stem: 'tagged one batch of phages' protein coats with radioactive sulfur and another batch's DNA with radioactive phosphorus'.
units.resolved: Claim now: in Hershey and Chase’s experiment the phage’s DNA, not its coat, entered the bacteria, evidence its genes were DNA. Stem now describes two separately labelled batches and asks which tag turned up mostly inside.

units.evidence: [W5.2] 'killed ... virulent strain type III-S, when injected along with living but non-virulent type II-R pneumococci, resulted in a deadly infection'; [W5.12]
units.note: The setup does not give the learner the evidence the reveal relies on. Nothing in the stem rules out 'The heat-killed bacteria came back to life': that is excluded only by Griffith's control (heat-killed smooth bacteria alone did not kill and yielded no live bacteria), which the explain asserts ('Heat-killed bacteria don't revive') but the stem omits. The item is won by background knowledge, not by reasoning from the case. Claim 'can carry a gene' is a modern reading (fine).
units.fix: Add to the stem: 'Mice given either kind alone survived, and no live bacteria grew from the heat-killed ones.'
units.resolved: Stem now gives the controls: injected alone, neither the rough bacteria nor the heat-killed smooth ones killed mice ([W5.12]: fatal infection normally only from live virulent bacteria).

units.evidence: [W9.8] 'the hydrogen bonds themselves do not have a particularly significant impact on molecular stability, which is instead caused mainly by ... base stacking'; [W9.13]; [W2.25]; [W9.40] [W9.41]
units.note: Key, claim and the PCR use are right. The explain puts '3 hydrogen bonds vs 2' directly before 'needs more heat', presenting the textbook misconception that the cited GC-content source explicitly refutes: stability comes mainly from G–C stacking, not the extra hydrogen bond.
units.fix: Explain: 'G–C pairs hold together more strongly than A–T pairs, mainly because they stack more strongly on their neighbours (they also have three hydrogen bonds to A–T's two), so DNA with more G–C pairs needs more heat to separate. ...'
units.resolved: Explanation now leads with stronger G–C stacking as the main reason (GC-content source), with the three-versus-two hydrogen bonds in parentheses.
